name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 5 No 27

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

entries.clue: Wing broken from movement might linger with support (8,5)

indicatorNotes.might: What might be so is not fixed, so the words after it are only a possible arrangement of their letters and may be set down in another.

blocks.note: thirteen letters to be re-set, exactly the count the grid wants

annotation.surface: A faction that has walked out of a campaign may survive if people back it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Support' is the trap: a splint is a support, and a broken wing is the very thing you splint, so the word reads as part of the picture rather than as fodder. The definition runs to four words.
annotation.definitionFit: A splinter group is what a party calls the faction that has broken away and set up on its own; a wing is that faction while it is still attached.

entries.clue: Sostenuto pianoforte section sounds moreish (7)

indicatorNotes.section: A section of a thing is a piece cut out of it with its parts still in place, so a run of letters comes out of the words in front unbroken.

blocks.note: seven letters run straight on across the join between the two musical words

annotation.surface: A sustained passage on the piano that leaves you wanting more.
annotation.walkthrough: Thomas More invented Utopia in his book of 1516, so what the definition wants you to hear is More-ish; the biscuit sense, meaning you cannot stop eating, is the decoy. Sostenuto is the instruction to hold notes out.
annotation.definitionFit: Utopian means of More's Utopia, so the word said aloud — More-ish — is the definition, while its everyday sense of tempting a second helping is not.

entries.clue: One hundred and ten has entry to deal with (7)

indicatorNotes.entry: Gaining entry is getting inside, so the word before it goes in between the two pieces already standing side by side.

blocks.note: C is the Roman hundred
the clue's own word, taken at face value
the number spelt out rather than set in figures

annotation.surface: A figure of a hundred and ten getting itself written into the books.
annotation.walkthrough: Reading 'One hundred and ten' as a single number is the trap; it is the Roman C standing beside a spelt-out TEN, with room left between them for a visitor. To say you will deal with someone is to promise to chasten them.
annotation.definitionFit: To deal with a person, in the threatening sense a parent or a sergeant means it, is to chasten them — to take them down a peg by correction.

entries.clue: Constant, firm and beginning to tie knot (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: A word's beginning is the letter it opens with, so only that one letter is taken from what follows.

blocks.note: pi, the ratio of a circle to its diameter, is mathematics' best-known constant
a firm is a company, which writes itself Co in its own name
the first letter of the word, which is what the instruction in front asks for

annotation.surface: Something steady and businesslike, just starting to be tied up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Constant' looks like the adjective going with 'firm' and is a noun, which is where the clue turns. PI and CO are two of the commonest small pieces in the language of crosswords, worth owning outright.
annotation.definitionFit: A picot is the small ornamental loop knotted into the edge of lace, braid or crochet, so it is a knot in the needleworker's sense of the word.

entries.clue: Such a college adopts Israeli flyers etc., or other admission (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is an adjective and 'Such a college' is a noun phrase: the setter names the compound the word belongs to and leaves the solver to supply the missing half of it.

indicatorNotes.adopts: A family that adopts takes someone into itself, so the letters in front open up and hold what comes next inside them.
indicatorNotes.other admission: An admission is a way in, and calling it another one says the letters arrive inside in a different order from the one they were given in.

blocks.note: El Al is Israel's national airline, so its aircraft are the flyers meant
five letters to be re-set, and 'or' is two of them rather than a choice

annotation.surface: A college taking in an Israeli airline's staff and whoever else applies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Etc., or' reads as the setter trailing off and is five of the nine letters, which is the whole difficulty of the clue. The electoral college is the body of delegates that actually chooses an American president.
annotation.definitionFit: An electoral college is a body that votes on everybody else's behalf, so the adjective is what turns a plain college into that particular kind.

entries.clue: A lower height in South Wales (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a place name, so the setter locates it rather than defining it: 'in South Wales' says where Neath is instead of what the word means.

blocks.note: a neat is an ox or a cow, and a cow is a beast that lows
h = height, as on the dimensions printed on a parcel

annotation.surface: A modest hill somewhere in the south of Wales.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'A lower height' as a smaller hill. A lower is a beast that lows, which is a neat — the old word for cattle, surviving in neatsfoot oil. Neath stands at the mouth of its own river near Swansea.
annotation.definitionFit: Neath is a market town in Glamorgan, up the coast from Swansea, so the clue places the answer on the map rather than paraphrasing it.

entries.clue: Papal agreement with string attached for starters (9)

indicatorNotes.for starters: What comes first is the starter, so only the opening letters of the word in front are wanted.

blocks.note: con is Italian for with, as in con brio at the head of a score
a cord is a length of string
the opening two letters of the word, which is what the instruction after it asks for

annotation.surface: A deal with the Vatican that has conditions attached to it.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom behind the surface is 'no strings attached', which makes 'string' read as a condition rather than as a cord. A concordat is the treaty a pope signs with a state; Napoleon's of 1801 is the one the history books use.
annotation.definitionFit: A concordat is the formal agreement a pope concludes with a secular government, settling how the church is to stand in that country.

entries.clue: Old English Parliamentarian left army without male model (9)

indicatorNotes.without: A thing without something has had it taken away, so the letter named next is dropped from the word in front.

blocks.note: an ex-minister is the old one
E is English on a dictionary label
a Member of Parliament puts MP after his name
L is left, as stamped inside a pair of boots
ARMY gives up one letter, and the next block says which
M is male on a form — the letter the army loses

annotation.surface: A long-ago English MP who walked out of an army that had no men in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Model' is the definition and not the noun it looks like: a model pupil is an exemplary one. The rest is five pieces stacked, four of them standing abbreviations, with the army docked of its male at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A model pupil, or a model husband, is the one held up as the example everyone else should follow, which is what exemplary means.

entries.clue: Transgression strange to the ears of the church council (5)

indicatorNotes.to the ears: What reaches the ears is heard rather than read, so the two words in front are wanted for the noise they make and not for their spelling.

blocks.note: a transgression is a sin, and said aloud that vowel can be written the other way
strange is odd, and a doubled D is heard as a single one

annotation.surface: A sin that strikes the church council as peculiar.
annotation.walkthrough: One sound instruction governing two separate words is the unusual part: each is respelt by ear before the two are joined. The Church of England's General Synod has met twice a year since 1970.
annotation.definitionFit: A synod is the assembly of bishops and clergy that sits to settle a church's affairs, which is exactly what a church council does.

entries.clue: Might Hector grouse and Tommy scoff? (5-4)

blocks.note: to hector somebody is to browbeat them, from the Trojan prince whose name became a word for a swaggerer
to grouse is to complain, and the slang noun for a grumble is also a butcher's word

annotation.surface: Wondering whether Hector will grumble and Tommy will eat.
annotation.walkthrough: Both capitals are people in the surface and something else underneath: Hector is a name and a way of bullying, Tommy is the ordinary British private soldier. Bully beef is the tinned corned beef he lived on in the trenches.
annotation.definitionFit: Bully beef is the tinned salt beef issued to British troops, and scoff is army slang for food, so a Tommy's scoff is that tin.

entries.clue: Pipe lines — that’s right (5)

blocks.note: British Rail ran the nationalised railway lines from 1948 until privatisation in the 1990s
i.e. is short for id est, the Latin for that is
R is right, as in a stage direction

annotation.surface: Somebody confirming a guess about pipelines.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is one word, and printing 'Pipe lines' as two invites you to read pipeline and lose it. A brier pipe is turned from the root burl of the white heath that grows round the Mediterranean.
annotation.definitionFit: A brier is the briar pipe — the bowl cut from the root of the tree heath, the standard material a smoker's pipe is made of.

entries.clue: Halt work: nothing grey-green and greasy here! (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a quotation rather than a synonym: Kipling's adjectives are so firmly attached to this river that they name it on their own, and 'here' marks the answer as a place.

blocks.note: to halt, in its old sense, is to walk lame
op is short for opus, a composer's numbered work
the letter O standing in for the figure nought

annotation.surface: A foreman calling a stop because there is nothing slimy to be found.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Halt' is the old adjective for lame — 'the halt and the blind' — and to go halt is to limp. The adjectives are Kipling's: the Elephant's Child goes to the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo, all set about with fever-trees.
annotation.definitionFit: Kipling's Just So Stories send the Elephant's Child to 'the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River', and those adjectives have named that African river ever since.

entries.clue: Errant policemen taking a day-return (7)

indicatorNotes.return: Something on its return journey is heading back the way it came, so the letters assembled in front of the word are written out right to left.

blocks.note: the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes branch of a British police force
the clue's own letter, taken as it stands
Mon is the diary short form of Monday, the day the rest of the assembly settles on

annotation.surface: Wayward officers buying themselves a cheap ticket for the day.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'day-return' is the misdirection: a day return is a railway ticket, and here its two halves do different jobs, one naming Monday and the other turning the whole assembly round. Errant means wandering, not mistaken.
annotation.definitionFit: Errant in its oldest sense is wandering — a knight errant roams the country — and a nomadic people is one that keeps no fixed home.

entries.clue: Sport involving e.g. roach’s finis (6,7)

indicatorNotes.involving: To involve things is to tangle them together — an involved explanation is a knotted one — so the letters named next come out in a new order.

blocks.note: thirteen letters to be re-set, 'e.g.' among them as two plain letters

annotation.surface: A sport that carries on down to the very last roach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Finis' is the word printed at the end of an old book, so it looks like an instruction to take a final letter; it is five of the thirteen instead. Coarse fishing is angling for everything except salmon and trout.
annotation.definitionFit: Coarse fishing is the British angler's sport of taking freshwater fish other than salmon and trout, roach and bream and tench among them.

entries.clue: Quiet oracle or unquiet conventual (4,5)

indicatorNotes.unquiet: An unquiet thing will not stay still, so the letters in front of the word refuse to keep the order they were given in.

blocks.note: p is piano, the musician's mark for quiet
eight letters to be re-set behind the first one

annotation.surface: A choice offered between a soft-spoken prophet and a restless nun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' and 'unquiet' look like a matched pair and do quite different jobs, one giving a letter and the other moving the rest. The Poor Clares are the Franciscan second order, founded by St Clare of Assisi in 1212.
annotation.definitionFit: A conventual is a member of a convent, and a Poor Clare is a nun of the enclosed Franciscan order that St Clare founded.

entries.clue: Prince Mishkin? The same! Nothing in it (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is by example, which the question mark admits: Prince Mishkin is one particular holder of the title rather than a synonym for the word.

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts one thing inside another, so the letter named before it goes between the two letters of the word named after.

blocks.note: id. is short for idem, Latin for the same, used in footnotes to save repeating a source
the clue's own word, and the one that opens up
a nought written as the letter O

annotation.surface: Somebody naming a prince and adding that there is nothing in him.
annotation.walkthrough: Dostoevsky's Prince Myshkin, the holy innocent of the 1869 novel, gives the definition by example. 'The same' is the id. of footnotes, short for idem, and one of the smallest conventions worth owning.
annotation.definitionFit: Prince Mishkin is the title character of Dostoevsky's The Idiot, an epileptic innocent whose goodness everyone mistakes for simplicity, so naming him names the word.

entries.clue: Some of the colour of one’s money. Get most! (5)

indicatorNotes.most: Most of a word is nearly all of it and not quite all, so the last letter comes off what the instruction points at.

blocks.note: tin is Victorian slang for cash, still heard in 'a nice bit of tin'
the word loses its last letter, which is what the instruction after it asks for

annotation.surface: The shade of the cash in your pocket, and an order to grab as much of it as you can.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The colour of one's money' is the idiom the surface leans on, and the clue cuts it in half: the first words define, the rest are letters. Tin for money dates from the 1830s and has outlived most of its rivals.
annotation.definitionFit: A tinge is a trace of colour washed over something else — some of a colour rather than the whole of it.

entries.clue: Note the 1346 battle, admitting an instance of desertion (9)

indicatorNotes.admitting: To admit somebody is to let them in at the door, so the word in front opens up and takes the letters after it inside.

blocks.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
Crécy, in Picardy, is where Edward III's archers destroyed the French cavalry in August 1346
the clue's own word goes in whole

annotation.surface: Noting the battle of 1346 and allowing that one lot of men ran away.
annotation.walkthrough: Giving the year instead of the name is the point: 1346 belongs to one battle and nothing else, so the date is as good as a name. Recreancy is the noun for turning coward — a recreant knight has broken faith and fled.
annotation.definitionFit: Recreancy is cowardly desertion of a cause, a faith or a flag: the behaviour of a man who has gone back on his word and run.

entries.clue: Note the battles with one’s impressions (9)

blocks.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
an action is an engagement between forces, as in 'killed in action'

annotation.surface: Taking note of the fighting along with what people made of it.
annotation.walkthrough: This is 5 down again with the year taken out, and the two clues open on the identical words before going different ways. An action is a battle in the military sense, which is where the plural comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Your reactions to a piece of news are the impressions it leaves on you — what you make of it once it has sunk in.

entries.clue: Don Lenin’s dentures! Put out SOS! Repolish! That’s the Berliners’ way! (5,3,6)

indicatorNotes.Put out: Something put out has been shown the door, so the three letters named beside the phrase leave the pile before anything else is done.
indicatorNotes.Repolish: To polish a thing a second time is to work it over until it comes up looking different, which is what happens to the letters that are left.

blocks.note: seventeen letters to work from, three more than the grid has room for
the distress call's own three letters are the ones that go

annotation.surface: A barked run of orders about Lenin's false teeth, a distress call and a spot of polishing.
annotation.walkthrough: Three exclamation marks disguise the fact that each phrase is a separate instruction rather than part of one rant. Unter den Linden — 'under the lime trees' — runs east from the Brandenburg Gate, so 'way' means a street.
annotation.definitionFit: Unter den Linden is the boulevard that runs through the middle of Berlin from the Brandenburg Gate, so it is literally a way belonging to Berliners.

entries.clue: Stocking up with it (9-4)

blocks.note: read as laying in a store of goods, and meant as one stocking held up off the floor
read as the thing you are laying in, and meant as naming the article the holding up is done with

annotation.surface: Somebody laying in a store of something while there is still time.
annotation.walkthrough: There is nothing here to take apart into letters: four words carry two readings and the hyphen in the enumeration is the only hint that a single compound article is wanted. Stockings were held up this way until tights arrived in the 1960s.
annotation.definitionFit: A suspender-belt is the band worn at the waist whose straps clip to a stocking and keep it up, so the whole clue describes the job it does.

entries.clue: Thus charged Id finance petrol dealing? No no! (8,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is adverbial where the answer is a noun: 'thus charged' says how a bill has been made out, and the answer is the figure written on it.

indicatorNotes.dealing: Dealing is what you do to a pack of cards — the same items come round again in a different order — so the letters in front are redistributed.

blocks.note: fifteen letters to work from, two more than are wanted
the second no cancels the first: there is to be no NO in the pile, so those two letters come out

annotation.surface: An indignant refusal to bankroll the petrol trade at the going rate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Id' looks like Freud's and is two letters of the fodder; the closing 'No no!' is an instruction rather than an outburst, saying the pile must contain no NO. Everything between them is raw material.
annotation.definitionFit: A price that has been inflated is one blown up well past what the goods are worth, which is what being charged in that manner comes to.

entries.clue: An intoxicating time between strokes? (5,4)

blocks.note: somebody a drink or two in is described this way, a sense the word has carried since the eighteenth century
a striking clock marks off the stretch from one chime to the next

annotation.surface: A merry spell of time in between the chimes of a clock.
annotation.walkthrough: The clock is what makes the sentence work twice over: read straight it describes the pub's early-evening cut-price stretch, and read as wordplay it hands over two pieces. Drinkers have called that stretch this since the American navy of the 1920s.
annotation.definitionFit: Happy hour is the pub's early-evening spell of cheap drink, so the whole clue reads straight: an hour, measured out by a clock's strokes, that leaves its drinkers merry.

entries.clue: Gooseberry, peach or nectarine’s beginnings (9)

indicatorNotes.beginnings: The beginnings of a word are the letters it opens with, so the front of the word before it is taken and the rest left behind.

blocks.note: seven letters to be re-set, and 'or' is two of them rather than a choice between fruit
the opening two letters of the word, as the instruction after it asks

annotation.surface: Three fruits offered in a row, the last of them only just started.
annotation.walkthrough: Playing gooseberry puts the definition among the fruit, which is why the list reads so smoothly and hides so well. 'Or' looks like the word offering you a choice and is two of the nine letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To play gooseberry is to be the unwanted third tagging along with a courting couple, which is a chaperone's duty done by somebody who was not asked.

entries.clue: See 7
Dance between Dis World and De Next (5)

annotation.definition2: between Dis World and De Next
annotation.definitionNote: The second definition names a place rather than describing a thing, and the setter spells 'this' and 'the' in Caribbean speech so that the two halves share one voice.

blocks.note: the West Indian floor dance in which you bend backwards to pass under a bar lowered a notch each time

blocks.clueFragment: between Dis World and De Next
blocks.note: the borderland of old Catholic teaching, neither heaven nor hell; Dis is the walled city of Dante's Inferno too

annotation.surface: A dance performed somewhere between this world and the next one.
annotation.walkthrough: The patois spelling does two jobs at once: it points at the Caribbean the dance comes from, and it lets Dis stand as the name of Dante's infernal city. The place held unbaptised infants and the virtuous pagans.
annotation.definitionFit: Limbo is the Trinidadian dance under a lowered bar, and Limbo is also the theological border-country for souls shut out of heaven without being damned.

entries.clue: Mushroom cloud causes soldier to follow diversion (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is plural and 'mushroom' alone is not: 'cloud' supplies the multitude, a whole crop of them at once, while the nuclear phrase hides that reading.

indicatorNotes.to follow: What follows comes after, so the piece named before the phrase is placed second, behind the one named after it.

blocks.note: a diversion is something laid on to amuse
GI is the American private, from the 'government issue' stamped on his kit

annotation.surface: A nuclear blast sending a soldier off after a distraction.
annotation.walkthrough: The mushroom cloud of the surface is the bomb's, and the clue wants a cloud of mushrooms instead, which is where the plural comes from. GI is the 'government issue' stamped on American army kit.
annotation.definitionFit: Fungi is the plural of fungus, the family mushrooms belong to, so a cloud of mushrooms is simply a mass of them together.

entries.clue: Some album photographs bound with red tape? (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a thing is a part of it taken as it stands, so a run of letters is lifted unbroken out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: five letters run on unbroken across the join between the two words

annotation.surface: Snapshots out of an album done up in a red ribbon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bound with red tape' reads as a parcel of photographs tied with ribbon, which is what hides the definition: the tape is the bureaucrat's. The word is army slang, a polite shortening of bum fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Bumph is the useless paperwork a bureaucracy turns out — memos, forms and circulars — which is red tape in the form you can pick up and weigh.
